mathgap.title: Sequential processing of transfers
mathgap.principle: When a transfer statement appears, immediately adjust the giver's and receiver's counts before processing any subsequent statements, because later statements refer to the updated counts. Failing to do this leaves later constraints based on outdated values.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever you encounter a statement of the form "X gives K items to Y" (or similar transfer).
mathgap.example: After a transfer X gives 3 items to Y, later statements still use X's original count as if the transfer never happened.

mathgap.title: Signed difference equality
mathgap.principle: For statements equating a signed difference to another difference, translate both sides as signed differences preserving the order of names as written: "A has N more than B" becomes (A - B) = N, and "the difference between the number of items that X and Y have" becomes (X - Y). Apply this to both sides of the equality. Mis‑ordering or treating the difference as absolute leads to contradictions.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When a statement contains phrases like "A has N more than B" or "the number of items that A has more than B is equal to the difference between the number of items that C and D have".
mathgap.example: Interpreting "the difference between the number of blueberries that Hayward and Lucille have" as |Hayward - Lucille| or as (Lucille - Hayward) instead of (Hayward - Lucille), causing an inconsistent equation.

mathgap.title: Direct count assignment at point of mention
mathgap.principle: When a statement directly gives a count for a person (e.g., "X has N items"), set that person's current count to N at that point, overwriting any previous value. Later statements refer to this updated count. Ignoring the new assignment leaves you with an outdated value.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever a statement explicitly states a person's count.
mathgap.example: Ignoring a later direct count "Z has 12 items" and keeping Z's earlier value, causing later equations to use the wrong number.

mathgap.title: Update both parties in a transfer
mathgap.principle: For a transfer "X gives K items to Y", subtract K from X's current count and add K to Y's current count. Both sides must be updated; updating only the receiver inflates the total number of items.
mathgap.example: Adding K to the receiver's count after "Berdie gives 6 blueberries to Rafael" but forgetting to subtract 6 from Berdie's count, resulting in too many blueberries overall.

mathgap.title: Systematic linear solving
mathgap.principle: After translating all statements into algebraic equations, collect them into a linear system and solve for the unknowns using substitution, elimination, or matrix methods. This ensures all constraints are satisfied simultaneously. Guessing values without solving can miss dependencies.
mathgap.when_to_apply: After parsing all statements and before answering the query.
mathgap.example: Trying to infer the queried person's count by intuition rather than solving the full set of equations, leading to an incorrect answer.

mathgap.title: Non‑negative integer check
mathgap.principle: All item counts must be non‑negative integers. If solving yields a negative or fractional value, the interpretation of the statements is likely wrong; revisit sign handling or order. Accepting invalid values leads to impossible solutions.
mathgap.when_to_apply: After solving the system, before finalizing the answer.
mathgap.example: Accepting a solution where a person's count is -3 or 4.5, which cannot occur for whole items.

mathgap.title: Split operation handling
mathgap.principle: When a person splits all their items equally among two recipients, set the giver's count to zero and give each recipient half of the original amount (the total must be even). This reflects the described operation. Leaving the giver with the original count double‑counts the items.
mathgap.when_to_apply: For statements like "X splits all the items she owns equally among Y and Z."
mathgap.example: After "X splits all the tomatoes she owns equally between Y and Z", leaving X with its original count instead of zero, resulting in too many tomatoes overall.

mathgap.title: Conditional transfer handling
mathgap.principle: For statements of the form "If X has more than N items, X will transfer their items to Y", first evaluate the condition using X's current count; if true, move all of X's items to Y (X becomes zero, Y gains X's count). Performing the transfer regardless of the condition violates the problem's logic.
mathgap.example: Transferring items from X to Y even though X's count is not greater than the threshold N, thereby breaking the conditional rule.

mathgap.title: Redistribution equalization handling
mathgap.principle: When a statement says "X and Y redistribute their items to ensure each has an equal amount", pool their total items and give each half (the total must be even). Update both X and Y accordingly. Ignoring this step leaves the original unequal distribution unchanged.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When a redistribution equalization statement appears.
mathgap.example: Ignoring the equalization step for "Axel and Jonas redistribute their tomatoes to ensure each has an equal amount" and keeping their original counts, causing later equations to be off.

mathgap.title: Combined statements handling
mathgap.principle: When a statement involves multiple relational clauses or sums on one side (e.g., "X has 1 more than Y and 2 fewer than Z" or "X + Y = Z + W"), translate each clause into a separate linear equation, preserving signs and order. Treating them as a single equation can miss constraints.
mathgap.when_to_apply: For statements that contain sums or multiple relational clauses.
mathgap.example: Treating "Juan has 1 more tomato than Marina and 15 fewer tomatoes than Eugene" as a single equation instead of creating two equations (Juan = Marina + 1 and Juan = Eugene - 15), leading to an underdetermined system.

mathgap.description: Treating signed difference statements as absolute differences
mathgap.why_it_happens: The phrasing "has more than" suggests a magnitude, so the model defaults to an absolute difference.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Keep the sign and order: translate "A has N more than B" to A - B = N, not |A - B| = N.

mathgap.description: Ignoring the sequential order of transfers
mathgap.why_it_happens: The model treats transfers as independent constraints rather than actions that change state.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Apply each transfer immediately, updating both giver and receiver before processing later statements.

mathgap.description: Assuming explicit counts are final after all transfers
mathgap.why_it_happens: Direct counts are taken as immutable, overlooking later modifications.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Treat direct counts as setting the current value, which can later be changed by transfers or other actions.

mathgap.description: Updating only the receiver in a transfer
mathgap.why_it_happens: The model focuses on the recipient and forgets to subtract from the giver.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Subtract the transferred amount from the giver as well as adding it to the receiver.

mathgap.description: Reversing the direction in "X has N more than Y" statements
mathgap.why_it_happens: Confusion about which person is larger leads to swapping the equation.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Remember that "X has N more than Y" means X = Y + N.

mathgap.why_it_happens: The phrase is ambiguous; the model may default to absolute difference or reverse the order.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Always translate "the difference between A and B" as (A - B), preserving the order exactly as written.
